q: metallic taste people get after illness
metallic taste in mouth after being sick
why do I have metallic taste when sick
a: A metallic taste in the mouth (dysgeusia) that occurs after an illness can have several causes. During an upper respiratory infection (cold, flu, sinusitis), inflammation can affect the olfactory and gustatory systems, altering taste perception. The sinuses and nasal passages are closely connected to taste, and congestion can distort how flavors are perceived. Some medications used to treat illnesses, including antibiotics, antivirals, and decongestants, can cause a metallic taste as a side effect. Respiratory infections can also cause zinc deficiency or alter zinc metabolism, and zinc plays a crucial role in taste function. Certain viral infections like COVID-19 have been strongly associated with taste disturbances, including metallic or distorted taste (parosmia and dysgeusia), due to the virus affecting olfactory receptors and nerve cells. Other causes include sinus infections (bacterial sinusitis can produce metallic-tasting post-nasal drip), allergies, and certain autoimmune conditions. The metallic taste typically resolves as the underlying illness clears, though it can persist for weeks or months in some cases, particularly after viral infections.
